Immunosuppression in Decompensated Autoimmune Hepatitis Cirrhosis: To Suppress or Not to Suppress?
  • Source: Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics, 2026; Vol. 0:1–22
  • Topic: Management of immunosuppression in AIH patients with decompensated cirrhosis, balancing therapy against liver transplantation
  • Author(s): Pedro Robson Costa Passos, Valbert Oliveira Costa Filho, Guilherme Grossi Lopes Cançado
1. Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) Overview
  • Chronic liver disease with variable relapsing course
  • Predominantly affects women
  • Can range from mild inflammation to submassive necrosis
  • May present as acute liver failure in severe cases
  • Declining cirrhosis at presentation: 33% → ~10% in recent data [4–6]
  • 42% of patients experience fibrosis progression at follow-up [7, 8]
  • AIH-cirrhosis patients develop fewer decompensating events than other etiologies
  • Better prognosis after decompensation if complete biochemical remission (CBR) achieved [9, 10]
2. Clinical Dilemma in Decompensated AIH Cirrhosis
  • Central question: immunosuppress or prioritize liver transplantation (LT)?
  • Decompensated patients are highly susceptible to infections due to:
  • Cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction (CAID)
  • ↑ bacterial translocation
  • Portal hypertension-related complications
  • Immunosuppression risks: infections, treatment futility, delayed LT access
  • Potential benefits: attenuate inflammation, stabilize liver function
  • Paradoxical concern: ↓ MELD scores may complicate LT access without restoring true hepatic reserve [13, 14]
3. Immunological Mechanisms in AIH Cirrhosis
3.1 T-Cell Dysregulation
  • AIH is primarily a T-cell disease
  • Caused by loss of tolerance toward self-antigens
  • Regulatory T-cell (Treg) dysfunction → primary defect in function
  • Allows expansion of effector subsets, particularly Th1 cells
  • Th1 cells secrete: IFN-γ, IL-2 → induce HLA class I/II expression on hepatocytes [26–29]
  • ↑ IFN-γ stimulates CD8+ cytotoxic T cells → direct hepatocyte destruction [30]
  • TNF is the most upregulated cytokine in AIH liver specimens
  • TNF mediates tissue injury and apoptosis via macrophage/NK T-cell amplification [2, 31]
  • TNF-producing Th1 cells are selectively expanded in liver infiltrates [32]
3.2 Dual Immunological Niche
  • Intrahepatic niche: Th1-driven inflammation continues despite systemic paralysis
  • Local immune activation persists (89% have elevated aminotransferases) [41]
  • Intrahepatic T cells display more activation markers than controls [42]
  • Systemic niche: Peripheral immune paralysis
  • Translocation of enteric bacterial products → ↑ IFN-γ production by Th1-polarized cells [11, 33]
  • Rapid depletion of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in decompensated cirrhosis
  • ↑ CD4/CD8 ratio with Th1 expansion in mesenteric lymph nodes and peripheral blood [33, 34]
  • Despite inflammatory milieu → CD4+ T cells show strongly diminished cytokine production [35, 36]
  • This disconnect = main mechanism underlying CAID → predisposes to infections [12, 37]
3.3 Mechanisms Amplifying Intrahepatic Inflammation
  • IL-15 and IL-7 signals from liver-resident myeloid cells/hepatocytes → promote CD8+ T cell proliferation and cytotoxic differentiation [23]
  • MAdCAM-1 upregulation → enriches intrahepatic α4β7+ CD4+/CD8+ T cells and monocyte recruitment [43, 44]
  • DAMPs from hepatocyte death → drive inflammation in chronic liver disease [45, 46]
  • HLA class II+ hepatocytes can present autoantigens directly → amplify T-cell responses [47]
  • Reduced efferocytosis by dysfunctional Kupffer cells and LSECs → perpetuates inflammation [48–50]
  • DAMP-autoantibody complexes → ↑ activation of autoantigen-specific CD8+ T cells [51]
3.4 Therapeutic Implications
  • Immunosuppression mitigates ongoing liver injury BUT:
  • May exacerbate peripheral immune paralysis
  • Risk of infection → primary trigger for ACLF and leading cause of mortality [54, 55]
  • In established cirrhosis → liver dysfunction reflects fixed structural damage vs. ongoing immune-mediated injury
  • Substantial uncertainty whether benefits outweigh risks in "burnt-out" cirrhosis [56–58]
4. Immunosuppressive Therapy in Decompensated AIH
4.1 Standard Treatment Approach
  • First-line therapy: Predniso(lo)ne + azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil
  • Maintenance: steroid-sparing agent alone or low-dose predniso(lo)ne [15, 60–62]
  • Azathioprine avoided when initiating treatment in decompensated cirrhosis [15]
  • Concerns: severe cytopenias, idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, life-threatening infections
  • Prednisone typically preferred for treatment initiation [15]
  • No evidence-based recommendations for optimal dosing in this setting
4.2 Agent-Specific Considerations
  • Prednisone/Prednisolone
  • Universal first-line induction agent
  • Dosing varies widely: median 8 mg/day to 15–50 mg/day [14, 67]
  • ≥0.5 mg/kg/day used in 70% of patients in one series [41]
  • No consistent dose-response relationship established
  • Budesonide
  • Contraindicated in cirrhosis (portal-systemic shunting reduces first-pass clearance)
  • Associated with ↑ portal vein thrombosis risk [15]
  • Azathioprine
  • Avoid routine initiation at presentation in decompensated disease
  • May be considered later once clinical stabilization achieved
  • Mycophenolate mofetil
  • Reasonable steroid-sparing option once clinically stable
  • Evidence in decompensated cirrhosis is indirect [60–62]
  • Tacrolimus
  • Used mainly in refractory/difficult-to-treat AIH
  • Target trough ~6 ng/mL [15]
  • Rituximab
  • Very limited evidence in AIH
  • Cannot be recommended for decompensated AIH cirrhosis [15]
  • Infliximab
  • Steroid-free TNF blockade can induce biochemical remission in newly diagnosed AIH [23, 52]
  • AASLD and EASL caution against use due to weak efficacy evidence and infection risk [15]
4.3 Infectious Complications
  • Infection rates: 26%–34.7% in immunosuppressed decompensated AIH patients
  • Surprisingly equivalent to untreated patients [14, 41, 68, 98]
  • Likely due to selection bias (less severe patients treated)
  • In Barbero study: 7/9 deaths in treated patients were attributed to infection [67]
  • Higher initial corticosteroid doses not associated with ↑ post-transplant infections in carefully selected candidates [41, 58]
4.4 Factors Predicting Poor Response
  • Moderate-to-severe ascites
  • Affects ~89% of patients at time of decompensation [41]
  • Associated with 15.73-fold increased hazard of LT or death [78]
  • Convergence of ascites + immunosuppression → particularly hazardous
  • Overt hepatic encephalopathy (OHE) grade ≥3
  • Most powerful predictor of poor TFS with immunosuppressive treatment [41]
  • Independent risk factor for de novo infections—even after adjustment [84]
  • High-grade OHE signals large spontaneous portosystemic shunts
  • Up to 65% of total hepatic blood flow diverted away from liver [87–89]
  • May alter drug pharmacokinetics → reduced intrahepatic levels, ↑ systemic exposure
4.5 Pharmacokinetic Concerns
  • Portosystemic shunting affects oral drug absorption
  • Splanchnic blood bypasses liver → reduced intrahepatic drug levels
  • Prednisone and azathioprine require hepatic metabolism to active forms [95]
  • ↓ cytochrome P450 enzyme activity in cirrhosis → variable drug disposition [96]
  • Budesonide concerns are well-established due to high first-pass metabolism [2, 97]
5. Predictors of Transplant-Free Survival (TFS)
5.1 MELD Score Thresholds
  • MELD-Na ≤22: reasonable chances of responding to treatment [14, 41]
  • MELD-Na ≤28: significantly better TFS in treated patients [41, 74]
  • MELD-Na ≥28: consistently associated with poor outcomes despite therapy [14, 41]
  • MELD-Na 23–27: "grey zone" requiring individualized decision-making
  • Relationship is continuous rather than binary [14, 68]
5.2 Other Prognostic Factors
  • Lower baseline albumin → poor prognosis
  • Higher AST/ALT levels at baseline → may reflect more reversible immune-mediated injury [41, 67, 126]
  • Male sex → associated with better outcomes in some studies [67]
  • Higher hemoglobin and WBC count at baseline → associated with recompensation [67]
5.3 Decompensating Event Type
  • Ascites as sole decompensating event → HR 14.40 (95% CI 4.17–49.64) for recompensation [126]
  • Variceal bleeding as first event → less likely to achieve recompensation
  • May be considered for immunosuppression trial if hemodynamically stable and no infection [145, 146]
  • Ascites + encephalopathy → poor response; prioritize LT
6. Response Assessment to Immunosuppression
6.1 Dynamic Monitoring Timepoints
  • Week 1 assessment: Early biochemical trends may provide preliminary insight
  • MELD reduction of 1.5 points → associated with treatment response (78.6% sensitivity) [67]
  • Total bilirubin reduction > 0.196 mg/dL → associated with response (92.9% sensitivity) [67]
  • These thresholds remain insufficiently validated
  • Week 4 assessment: More robust evaluation recommended [41, 67]
  • MELD-Na reduction → each 1-point reduction = ~11% relative hazard reduction for LT/death [41]
  • ≥50% transaminase reduction from baseline → correlates with ↑ LT-free survival
  • 92% vs. 64% at 12 months; 88% vs. 53% at 36 months [41]
  • MELD-Na reduction ≥11 points → 100% negative predictive value for death/LT [41]
6.2 Stop Rules and Early Identification of Non-Responders
  • Failure to achieve significant reduction in bilirubin or MELD-Na by week 4 → prompt immediate LT referral
  • High risk of unfavorable outcomes if treatment continued without response
  • SURFASA score (for acute severe AIH): incorporates baseline INR + % changes in INR/bilirubin over first 3 days
  • Highly predictive of response; excellent discrimination for LT/death [104, 105]
  • Cohort: 21% had cirrhosis at baseline; no data on prior decompensation [104]
6.3 Limitations of Standard Response Criteria
  • Aminotransferases and IgG are poor markers in decompensated cirrhosis [100–103]
  • Autoantibodies used mostly for diagnostic purposes
  • Need for response criteria specific to decompensated AIH
7. Liver Transplantation in AIH
7.1 LT Indications and Outcomes
  • 3%–5% of transplantations in Europe/USA for AIH [63, 109, 110]
  • Most common indication: decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatocellular failure
  • 10-year survival: ~80% [19, 112]
  • AIH patients generally have favorable prognosis post-LT
7.2 Recurrence Post-Transplant
  • ~21% recurrence rate according to recent meta-analysis [16]
  • Persistence of host Treg dysfunction → autoimmune process redirected toward allograft [113]
  • Unlike PBC, recurrent AIH associated with detrimental long-term outcomes [18, 115]
  • Requires more intensive chronic immunosuppression than standard post-LT protocols [116, 117]
7.3 Waitlist Considerations
  • 24% cumulative incidence of waitlist death/deterioration at 3 years [118]
  • Decision to transplant is highly time-sensitive
  • Current MELD-based allocation → concern that immunosuppression may artificially ↓ scores without proportional mortality/infection risk reduction [13]
  • No convincing data that treating AIH patients awaiting LT improves transplant likelihood or post-LT outcomes [109, 115]
7.4 Pre-LT Immunosuppression Concerns
  • Post-LT period: heightened susceptibility to infection and impaired wound healing [120, 121]
  • AIH patients are even more susceptible to post-LT infections and graft rejection [122]
  • Heavy pre-transplant immunosuppression may further compromise vulnerable postoperative phase
8. Recompensation in AIH Cirrhosis
8.1 Baveno VII Framework
  • Recompensation: partial regression of structural/functional changes after etiological removal [20]
  • Original consensus developed from alcohol-related and hepatitis B data
  • No accepted cure for AIH → treatment generally lifelong
  • Cessation → relapse in 50%–87% of adults and 60%–80% of children [123, 124]
  • Post-Baveno VII studies use CBR as proxy for etiological suppression [125, 126]
8.2 Recompensation Rates in AIH
  • ~25% of decompensated AIH patients recompensate (meta-analysis) [129]
  • Lower than alcohol-related (33%), hepatitis B (50%), hepatitis C (42%) [129]
  • Rates vary by definition used:
  • Simple absence of decompensation events: 62.5% [67]
  • Absence without prophylaxis: 49% [41]
  • Full Baveno VII criteria (clinical + CBR): 19%–34.6% [125, 126, 128]
  • Aggarwal exception (not using CBR): 53.6% [127] → excluded patients who decompensated while on immunosuppression
8.3 Predictors of Recompensation
  • Lower baseline IgG levels [126]
  • Higher ALT/AST levels at baseline [41, 67, 126]
  • Higher platelet count at baseline (HR 1.00) [126]
  • Ascites as sole decompensating event (HR 14.40) [126]
  • Lower Child-Turcotte Pugh score (HR 0.81) [127]
  • Younger age (sHR 0.98 per year) [127]
  • Lower baseline IL-17A, TNF-α, IFN-γ → less active inflammatory milieu [128]
  • Higher BMI (HR 1.161) and higher albumin → positive predictors [128]
  • Diabetes as negative predictor (HR 0.582) [128]
8.4 Post-Recompensation Outcomes
  • Lower mortality (HR 0.22) vs. non-recompensated [127]
  • Lower LT/death risk (HR 0.07) vs. non-recompensated [126]
  • Survival comparable to compensated patients [126]
  • 5.9%–15% experienced further decompensation after recompensation [127, 128]
  • 2-year incidence of re-decompensation: 8.5% [127]
8.5 Controversies in Recompensation Definition
  • CBR as proxy questioned because elevated immunoglobulins common in compensated cirrhosis [125, 134]
  • Histological activity persists despite normal ALT/IgG in considerable proportion of patients [135–137]
  • 57% of PBC-related decompensated cirrhosis eventually present with liver-related complications [143]
  • Debate: Should histology (mHAI ≤3) be required for true recompensation? [99, 125]
9. Clinical Decision Framework: To Suppress or to Transplant?
9.1 Patient Selection for Immunosuppression Trial
  • Contraindications to trial:
  • Active infection
  • ACLF or multiorgan dysfunction
  • These patients should undergo urgent LT evaluation [70, 144]
9.2 Risk Stratification by Decompensation Type
  • Moderate-to-severe ascites and/or OHE ≥grade 3 → poor response; prioritize LT
  • Mild ascites or low-grade OHE → consider short trial of immunosuppression
  • Isolated variceal bleeding (stabilized, no infection) → may be considered case-by-case
9.3 MELD-Na Stratification
  • ≤22: reasonable chance of responding → consider immunosuppression trial
  • 23–27 ("grey zone"): individualized expert assessment with strict stop rules
  • ≥28: unlikely to benefit → immediate LT evaluation
9.4 Proposed Treatment Algorithm
  • Step 1: Exclude active infection, ACLF, multiorgan dysfunction → urgent LT referral
  • Step 2: Assess decompensation type and MELD-Na score
  • Step 3: For selected candidates → time-limited trial with early response assessment
  • Week 1: Early monitoring for deteriorating patients in "grey zone"
  • Week 4: Robust assessment
  • MELD-Na reduction ≥2 points (clinically meaningful threshold)
  • ≥50% transaminase reduction
  • Stop rules: Failure to meet criteria → immediate LT referral
9.5 Key Limitations
  • All proposed response criteria derived from observational data
  • No prospective validation exists
  • Thresholds are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive
10. Future Research Directions
10.1 Pathophysiology
  • Characterize dual immune niche mechanisms using single-cell RNA sequencing and multiplex immunohistochemistry [152, 153]
  • Key questions:
  • What is the functional phenotype of intrahepatic T cells in decompensated AIH?
  • Does successful immunosuppression restore Treg function or merely suppress effector responses? [154, 155]
10.2 Biomarker Development
  • Validate existing early response criteria in large prospective cohorts
  • Develop novel biomarker panels:
  • Circulating inflammatory markers (e.g., cytokines)
  • Bacterial translocation markers (e.g., LPS-binding protein) [156–158]
  • Explore pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships in portosystemic shunting [159, 160]
10.3 Recompensation Definition
  • Determine if histologically-defined remission (mHAI ≤3) should be required for recompensation criteria
  • Long-term follow-up studies comparing clinical vs. histological recompensation definitions
10.4 Optimal Regimen Design
  • Are lower starting corticosteroid doses safer? [13, 162]
  • Does adding steroid-sparing agents from outset improve outcomes or increase toxicity? [163]
  • Role of emerging therapies (biologics targeting specific cytokines) for treatment failures [164]
10.5 Randomized Controlled Trials Needed
  • Central question (suppress vs. transplant) can only be definitively answered by prospective RCTs
  • Potential design: randomize "therapeutic window" patients (MELD-Na 23–27, no severe ascites/OHE) to:
  • Standardized immunosuppression with strict stop rules
  • Immediate LT listing with best supportive care
  • Would require large international consortium due to rarity of condition
11. Key Take-Home Points
  • 19%–31% of decompensated AIH patients achieve recompensation with immunosuppression
  • MELD-Na ≤28 and mild ascites predict treatment response
  • Moderate-to-severe ascites and OHE ≥grade 3 → poor prognosis; prioritize LT
  • Early dynamic response assessment at weeks 1 and 4 is critical for identifying non-responders
  • MELD-Na reduction ≥11 points at week 4 = 100% NPV for death/LT
  • MELD reduction of 1.5 points at week 1 = 78.6% sensitivity for response
  • Management requires individualized, protocolized strategy with strict stop rules
  • LT remains definitive treatment for end-stage AIH; excellent long-term outcomes (~80% 10-year survival)
  • Recurrence post-LT occurs in ~21% of cases
